title: Three & Four Pointer Extensions: kSum Family
summary: Fixing one or two elements with an outer loop and two-pointering the rest of a sorted array — the technique behind 3Sum, 3Sum Closest, and 4Sum.

slides.markdown:
[Opposite-end two pointers](opposite-end-two-pointers) solves pair-sum in O(n) on a sorted array. The kSum family — 3Sum, 3Sum Closest, 4Sum — extends that same converging-pointer core by wrapping it in one or two fixed outer loops.

The idea in one line: **fix the first k-2 elements with nested loops, then two-point the remaining two.** 3Sum fixes one element and two-points the rest; 4Sum fixes two and two-points the remaining pair. The converging-pointer core never changes — only how many elements sit outside it.

This turns an apparent O(n³) or O(n⁴) brute force into O(n²) or O(n³), because the innermost step is always the O(n) two-pointer sweep, not another nested loop.

slides.sectionTitle: Fix one element, two-point the rest
slides.subTitle: Extending pair-sum to triples
slides.markdown:
3Sum asks: find every triplet summing to zero (or a target). Sort the array first, then for each index `i` from left to right, fix `arr[i]` and run the opposite-end two-pointer search for a pair summing to `target - arr[i]` in the subarray to its right.

```python
def three_sum_core(arr, i, target):
    left, right = i + 1, len(arr) - 1
    pair_target = target - arr[i]
    while left < right:
        s = arr[left] + arr[right]
        if s == pair_target:
            yield (arr[i], arr[left], arr[right])
            left += 1
            right -= 1
        elif s < pair_target:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
```

The outer loop over `i` costs O(n), and each iteration's two-pointer search costs O(n), giving O(n²) total — one order of magnitude better than the O(n³) brute force of checking every triple.

slides.subTitle: An outer loop plus an inner converging pair search
slides.markdown:
For `arr = [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]` looking for triplets summing to 0: fix `i = 1` (value -1), then run the pair search on `[-1, 0, 1, 2]` for pairs summing to 1. `left` starts at index 2 (-1), `right` at index 5 (2): sum is 1, a match — record `(-1, -1, 2)`, advance both. Now `left=3` (0), `right=4` (1): sum is 1, another match — record `(-1, 0, 1)`. Pointers cross, this outer iteration ends, `i` advances to 2.

![An outer index i with a left and right pointer converging over the subarray to its right, finding two matched triplets before i advances](assets/3sum-outer-and-inner-pointers.svg)

slides.sectionTitle: Skipping duplicates at the wrong point
slides.markdown:
A common bug: adding the outer-loop duplicate skip as `if nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue` unconditionally, including when `i == 0`. That reads `nums[-1]`, the *last* element of the array, comparing against the wrong value entirely — Python doesn't error on this since negative indices are valid, it just silently produces wrong behavior on the very first iteration.

A second common bug: skipping duplicates for `left` and `right` *before* checking whether the current sum matched, rather than after recording it. That erases legitimate triplets — if `nums[left] == nums[left+1]` doesn't necessarily mean the *pair* is a duplicate of one already found; it only becomes a duplicate concern once a match has actually been recorded at that combination.

The fix in both cases: guard the outer skip with `i > 0`, and only run the left/right skip loops **inside** the `s == 0` (or `s == pair_target`) branch, immediately after appending the result.

slides.subTitle: Tracking the best-so-far instead of exact matches
One more fixed loop around the same converging core

slides.markdown:
3Sum and 4Sum can also be solved by fixing all but the last element with nested loops and using a hashmap for the final lookup instead of two pointers.

| | Sort + two pointers | Fix k-1, hashmap for last element |
|---|---|---|
| Time (3Sum) | O(n²) | O(n²) |
| Space | O(1) extra (aside from output and sort) | O(n) for the hashmap |
| Handles duplicate triplets | Needs explicit skip logic, but naturally ordered | Needs explicit dedup — a set of sorted tuples, typically |
| Requires sorting | Yes | No |

Both are the same time complexity for 3Sum, so the deciding factor is usually space and how painful duplicate handling gets — the hashmap version needs to dedupe result tuples explicitly (often via a set), which the sorted two-pointer version gets closer to for free by construction.

A candidate who hasn't internalized the pattern will often start 3Sum by trying to nest three nested nested loops (O(n³)), or attempt a fresh hashmap-based approach they haven't fully thought through under time pressure — reinventing something that's actually just "pair-sum with one extra fixed loop wrapped around it."

The efficient recognition path: "I already know how to solve pair-sum on a sorted array in O(n) with two pointers. 3Sum is pair-sum with one element fixed and subtracted from the target, repeated for every choice of fixed element." That framing gets you to the O(n²) solution directly, without deriving two-pointer convergence logic twice.

The broader lesson for the kSum family: once you've derived the converging-pointer proof once, every further "kSum" variant is the same core wrapped in one more (or fewer) fixed loop — recognize the wrapper, don't re-derive the core.
